topic: How to use AI for competitor analysis at scale

article.title: We Tracked 41 Competitors With AI. Only Three Mattered.
article.meta_description: A performance director's playbook for AI competitor analysis at scale: the three layer stack, a scoring rubric, and where the whole thing breaks.
article.author: Jordan Cole
article.intro: AI is genuinely good at competitor analysis in exactly one way. It reads everything, constantly, and never gets bored. What it's bad at is telling you which of those things deserves your attention, and if you get that division of labor backwards you'll build an expensive machine that produces a very tidy pile of nothing. In March 2024 I inherited a $2.4M annual paid budget at a B2B SaaS client whose competitor deck had been assembled in Google Slides eleven months earlier. Two of the six "primary rivals" had been acquired. One had quietly pivoted out of the category entirely. The account team was still writing ad copy against a positioning statement that no longer existed anywhere on the internet.
article.intro2: So the argument I'll make here is unpopular with the people who sell competitive intelligence software: refresh rate beats analytical depth almost every time. A shallow read of what your rivals did last Tuesday is worth more than a beautiful 60 slide teardown of what they did last spring. AI is the only thing that makes weekly refresh affordable, and that's the actual reason to use it. Not the insights. The cadence.

sections.heading: Most Competitor Decks Are Archaeology, Not Intelligence
sections.content:
Think about what a traditional competitive audit costs. An analyst spends two weeks pulling screenshots, pricing pages, review counts, and ad examples. Then it goes into a deck, gets presented once, and rots. By the time anyone acts on it, the creative rotation it documented is three cycles old.

Meanwhile the things that actually move week to week are small and boring. Which ad variants a competitor is still running after 30 days. Whether their pricing page added a usage based tier. Whether they're hiring three enterprise AEs (they're moving upmarket) or two support reps (they're firefighting churn). Review velocity on G2. Whether they started bidding on your brand terms.

None of that requires a genius to interpret. It requires somebody to look every week, and no human is going to look every week across 40 companies without quitting. That's the whole job AI is doing here, and I'd rather be honest about it than pretend the model is producing strategy. The cost side has moved in your favor too: Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index found inference costs for GPT-3.5 level performance fell more than 280 fold between late 2022 and late 2024. Monitoring that was economically absurd two years ago is now a rounding error.

sections.heading: The Three Layer Stack I Build For Every Client
sections.content:
Every setup I've shipped that survived contact with a real team splits into collection, extraction, and judgment. Mixing them is how projects die.

Collection: dumb, scheduled, and cheap

No model involved. Just scrapers and APIs on a cron. The sources that consistently earn their keep:

  • Meta Ad Library and the Google Ads Transparency Center, both free, both with dates so you can compute creative longevity
  • Pricing, homepage, and top three landing pages, snapshotted weekly as raw HTML
  • Careers pages, which are the single most underrated leading indicator in B2B
  • Review sites, tracked as counts and rating deltas rather than text
  • SERP position for your 50 highest intent terms

Extraction: the model's actual job

Feed the model raw text and ask for structured output only. Never prose. I use a fixed JSON schema per source type, so a pricing page comes back as tiers, prices, seat minimums, and a change flag versus last week. The moment you let it write paragraphs, you've made something nobody reads.

Judgment: still you

The model flags changes. A human decides which ones alter the media plan. In my work with mid market SaaS accounts, roughly one flagged change in fifteen was worth a meeting. That ratio hasn't budged in two years, and if a vendor tells you their tool fixes it, they're selling. I've written more on the mechanics of running competitor analysis at scale if you want the plumbing detail.

sections.heading: Score Competitors Before You Analyze Them, Not After
sections.content:
Here's the mistake that cost me about six weeks. We started with 41 companies because the client's sales team named 41. Every one got the full pipeline. The output was 41 weekly change reports that nobody opened, because the signal from the three companies that shared real auction overlap was buried under 38 companies we'd never actually lost a deal to.

Now I score first, on four things: auction overlap (do we see them in impression share reports at all), win/loss mentions from the last two quarters of CRM notes, paid activity volume, and organic overlap on money keywords. Anything scoring low goes into a quarterly glance list. Only the top tier gets weekly extraction. Three companies made it. The report went from ignored to read by the CRO every Monday.

And honestly? I'm still not sure the scoring weights I use are right. A friend of mine who runs growth at a fintech tried the same rubric and told me auction overlap was almost useless in his category because half his real competitors don't buy search at all, they just own two podcasts. He might be right. I once spent a full afternoon building a beautiful dashboard tracking a "competitor" that turned out to be our own agency's white label landing pages, which the scraper had been dutifully monitoring for five weeks. Nobody caught it. I presented it. Twice.

sections.heading: Where This Falls Over
sections.content:
Three failure modes, all of which I've hit. First, models invent pricing. If a page renders tiers in JavaScript and your scraper grabs an empty shell, the model will cheerfully fill the gap with something plausible. Fix: require a verbatim quote from source text for every numeric field, and drop the field if there isn't one.

Second, ad libraries are not a spend estimate. They show what's running, not what's funded. Every tool that claims to estimate competitor budgets is modeling from impression samples, and in the accounts where I could check against known figures, the estimates were off by enough to make them useless for planning.

Third, the genuine debate: does knowing competitor creative help at all? There's a real argument that chasing rival ads pushes everyone toward the same sameness. My position is that competitor data belongs in your hypothesis backlog, never straight into production. Adoption is nearly universal now, with McKinsey's 2025 State of AI survey putting organizational AI use at 78 percent, which means the edge isn't having the tool. It's what you feed into a disciplined testing process, and that's exactly the discipline gap behind why most AI marketing experiments stall out.

article.conclusion: Do this today, in under an hour: pull your Meta Ad Library results for your top three rivals, export the ads with their launch dates, and sort by how long each has been live. Anything running past 45 days is a proven winner they're paying to keep alive. That single list, with no model involved yet, will give you more testable angles than the last competitive deck anyone sent you. Then decide whether it's worth automating weekly, and pair it with predicting customer lifetime value earlier so you know which of those angles is worth defending.
article.image_alt: Marketing analyst reviewing competitor ad data across two monitors showing charts and spreadsheets

faq.q: What tools do I need to monitor competitor ads automatically?
faq.a: Meta Ad Library and the Google Ads Transparency Center are free and cover most paid activity. Add a scheduled scraper for pricing and careers pages, then run the raw text through an LLM with a fixed JSON output schema. A working setup runs somewhere between $180 and $400 a month at small scale.

faq.q: Can AI estimate how much a competitor is spending on ads?
faq.a: Not reliably. Every estimate on the market is modeled from impression samples, and in accounts where I could compare against real reported figures the numbers were far enough off to be unusable for budget planning. Track creative volume and longevity instead, since both are observable facts.

faq.q: How many competitors should I actually track weekly?
faq.a: Three to five. Score candidates on auction overlap, CRM win/loss mentions, paid volume, and organic keyword overlap, then send everything below the top tier to a quarterly review. Weekly reports covering 40 companies get ignored, which makes the whole system worthless.

topic: How to prompt AI for landing page copy that converts

article.title: The 200-Word Prompt That Beat My $12,000 Copywriter
article.meta_description: Most AI landing page copy fails because the prompt is starved of evidence. Here is the input structure I use after running $10M+ in paid traffic.
article.author: Jordan Cole
article.intro: The prompt is the product. Ask a model to "write high-converting landing page copy for my SaaS" and you'll get something that reads like a 2016 template, because you handed it exactly what you'd hand a junior copywriter before firing them out of frustration. Last March I rebuilt a lead capture page for a mid-market HVAC franchise, and the winning version came out of a prompt that contained 47 lines of pasted sales-call transcript. It beat the agency-written control by 31% on form submits across roughly 9,400 sessions, and the model I used was the same one that had produced garbage the week before. Nothing changed except what I fed it.
article.intro2: I've run somewhere north of $10M in paid media, and the pattern holds across every account I've touched: the quality gap between AI copy and good human copy is almost entirely an input gap. Marketers treat the prompt like a search query. It's closer to a creative brief, and briefs have required fields. If you skipped the part where you learn how your customers actually talk, no model on earth will invent it for you.

sections.heading: Evidence In, Copy Out
sections.content:
Start with raw language, not your summary of it. Sales call transcripts, support tickets, Gong snippets, G2 reviews, the ugly one-star ones especially. I paste 300 to 600 words of unedited customer speech directly into the prompt and instruct the model to mine it for the exact phrasing, then write only in that register. The first time I did this for a B2B logistics client, the headline the model produced used the phrase "we stopped guessing where the truck was," which came verbatim from a churned customer's exit interview. No strategist would have written that sentence. It converted at 8.2% against a 4.9% control.

This matters because attention is thinner than your deck assumes. Nielsen Norman Group's reading research found people read roughly 20 to 28% of the words on an average page, and that number drops as the page gets longer (Nielsen Norman Group). You get one hero section and maybe one subhead of real attention. Generic copy burns both.

The related failure is the empty brief, which I've written about before in more detail: an empty prompt produces empty copy, and no amount of prompt-engineering syntax rescues it. Structure without substance is still nothing.

sections.heading: The Five Inputs I Never Ship Without
sections.content:
My working prompt runs about 200 to 400 words before the transcript block. It's boring and it's repeatable, which is the point. Every field exists because leaving it out cost me money at some stage.

  • Traffic source and the exact ad that sent them. Paste the headline and primary text. Message match is the single biggest lever on a cold-traffic page, and the model can't match a promise it hasn't seen.
  • The offer mechanics in plain terms. Price, contract length, what happens in the first 48 hours after they convert. Vague offers produce vague copy.
  • The number-one objection from actual sales calls. Not the one your founder thinks it is. Ask the closer.
  • Forbidden claims. Compliance language, competitor names, anything legal will strike. Cheaper to state upfront than to rewrite.
  • One conversion action, named. "Book a 15-minute audit" beats "drive conversions" every time.

Then I ask for three variants with deliberately different angles: one loss-framed, one status-quo-attack, one plain-spoken and boring. The boring one wins more often than I'd like to admit. Around 40% of the time in my tests, which still surprises me.

sections.heading: Where This Falls Apart
sections.content:
Here's the honest part... this doesn't fix a page with a broken offer. I've watched teams generate 14 headline variants for a product priced 3x above its nearest competitor with no differentiation story, and the copy was never the constraint. If your unit economics don't work, better words just help you lose money faster and with more style.

Speed is the other silent killer that no prompt touches. Google's mobile benchmark research found 53% of mobile visits get abandoned when a page takes longer than three seconds to load (Think with Google, 2018). Half your traffic never reads the headline you agonized over. There's also a whole category of structural problems that copy can't paper over, which I've broken down separately in the page elements that quietly kill conversions.

My friend Dev runs growth at a fintech and he tried my exact prompt framework last summer, and honestly? It flopped for him. Twice. Turned out his transcripts were all from onboarding calls with people who had already bought, so the model kept writing to a warm, convinced audience while his traffic was ice cold from Reddit. He rewrote the input using pre-sale discovery calls instead and it worked fine. I'm not fully sure the framework transfers cleanly to every category, especially anything with a long committee-driven buying cycle. It works reliably for the accounts I run. That's the strongest claim I'll make.

sections.heading: Score the Output Before Anyone Sees It
sections.content:
I run every generated page through the same four checks, and I'd argue this step matters more than the prompt itself. Does the headline make a specific claim a competitor couldn't copy-paste? Does the first 40 words name the reader's situation rather than the company's credentials? Is there one CTA, repeated, not four competing ones? Can a stranger tell what happens after they click?

Fail any of the four and I don't test it, I regenerate with a corrective instruction. Testing bad variants is how teams burn six weeks proving that two mediocre pages are statistically indistinguishable. Unbounce's benchmark work puts the median landing page conversion rate across industries around 6.6% (Unbounce Conversion Benchmark Report), which means you need real volume to detect small lifts. Only test swings.

And once the page starts producing volume, the bottleneck moves downstream fast. More leads at worse quality will make sales hate you, which is why I usually pair a page rebuild with a lead scoring system sales will actually trust. Conversion rate on its own is a vanity metric if the leads never close.

article.conclusion: Do this today: open your last five recorded sales calls, pull 400 words of unedited customer speech, and paste it into your next landing page prompt above everything else you'd normally write. Add one line telling the model to reuse that exact vocabulary and never substitute a smarter synonym. Generate three angles, kill any that don't pass the four checks, and put the survivor against your current page. You'll know inside two weeks whether your copy problem was ever a copy problem.

sources.name: Nielsen Norman Group - How Little Do Users Read?
Think with Google - Mobile Page Speed Benchmarks

faq.q: How long should a landing page copy prompt be?
faq.a: Mine run 200 to 400 words of instruction plus 300 to 600 words of pasted customer language. Shorter than that and the model fills the gaps with generic SaaS filler. Length isn't the goal, specificity is, but specificity takes words.

faq.q: Which AI model writes the best landing page copy?
faq.a: The difference between top-tier models is far smaller than the difference between a starved prompt and a fed one. I use Claude for long-form and voice matching, but I've gotten winning pages out of three different models in the same month using identical inputs.

faq.q: Can AI replace a conversion copywriter?
faq.a: It replaces the drafting hours, not the judgment. Someone still has to pick the offer angle, run the customer interviews, and decide which variant is worth spending traffic on. I write prompts faster than I write copy, and I still throw away most of what comes back.

topic: AI-generated vs human-written email sequences - the open rate data

article.title: Apple Broke Open Rates. Your AI Email Test Is Lying
article.meta_description: AI-generated vs human-written email sequences: what open rate data really shows once you strip out Apple's fake opens, plus the metrics that predict revenue.
article.author: Alex Merritt
article.intro: AI-written email sequences usually post higher open rates than human-written ones, and that gap is mostly fake. In March 2024 I ran a 6-email welcome flow for a DTC supplement brand in Klaviyo, split 50/50 between GPT-written subject lines and lines written by a copywriter I'd paid for four years. The AI arm came in at 41.2% opens versus 36.8%. I nearly wrote the case study that afternoon. Then I filtered out Apple Mail Privacy Protection opens and the AI arm's real number dropped to about 22%, the human arm to 24%, and revenue per recipient favored the human arm by $0.31.
article.intro2: That's the pattern I've watched repeat across roughly a dozen accounts since. AI writes subject lines that trip more automated opens and more curiosity clicks from low-intent segments. Humans write body copy that survives the first four seconds after the click. If you're judging the two on opens alone, you're grading with a ruler that Apple snapped in half back in 2021, and the AI arm benefits from the break more than your writer does.

sections.heading: The 41% Open Rate That Meant Nothing
sections.content:
When Apple shipped Mail Privacy Protection with iOS 15, it started pre-fetching tracking pixels for Apple Mail users whether or not anyone read the message. Apple announced it in Apple Newsroom and the industry mostly shrugged. It shouldn't have. Apple Mail sits at a large share of tracked email opens according to Litmus client market data, which means a big slice of every open rate you report is a machine, not a person.

So why does the AI arm inflate more? Because the phantom opens land proportionally on whichever variant gets sent to more Apple users, and AI subject lines tend to get pushed into broader sends and larger audiences during testing. Add the fact that AI variants are often generated in batches of 20 and cherry-picked on early open data, and you've built a machine for selecting the variant that best flatters a corrupted metric.

Benchmarks don't rescue you either. The averages published by Mailchimp jumped noticeably after 2021 for the same reason, not because email suddenly got better. I dug into the underlying split by segment in more detail in this breakdown of what the AI versus human open rate data actually shows.

sections.heading: Where AI Actually Beat My Copywriters
sections.content:
I'm not here to defend artisanal email. AI won real ground in three places, and I've stopped arguing about them.

  • Volume of viable variants. A good writer gives me 5 subject lines an hour. Claude gives me 40 in ninety seconds, and maybe 6 are genuinely usable. That's still a better usable-per-hour rate.
  • Segment-level rewriting. Taking one proven email and rewriting it for 9 personas is grunt work. AI does it at near-parity with humans on click-to-open.
  • Re-engagement and transactional-adjacent flows. Low emotion, high clarity. In my work with a B2B SaaS client last year, the AI-written win-back sequence outperformed the human one on reply rate by about 12%, which surprised me enough that I re-ran it.

The pattern I've seen is that AI wins where the job is compression and consistency, and loses where the job is a specific point of view. That maps to what showed up when I compared tool outputs head to head in these real A/B tests of AI copywriting tools. Nobody's tool was bad. They were all just fluent in the same slightly weightless way.

sections.heading: Where It Lost, and Why the Loss Compounds
sections.content:
Unsubscribes. Every single time. Across the flows I've measured, AI-written sequences ran an unsubscribe rate somewhere between 15% and 30% higher than the human-written control, and the gap widened by email four. Nobody notices this in a two-week test. It shows up in month five when your sendable list is 8% smaller than your forecast.

Ok so, slightly embarrassing story. My friend Devin runs email for a mid-size pet brand and he swore AI subject lines were carrying his whole program. I told him he was measuring MPP noise. He told me I was being precious about it. We bet dinner on it, he pulled his numbers by client, and... he was half right? On his Gmail-heavy segment the AI lines genuinely won, no filtering trick involved. I'm honestly not 100% sure why. Best guess is his human copy was just tired, because it had been in market for eleven months untouched. So the AI wasn't beating a copywriter, it was beating a copywriter's old work. I paid for dinner. It was $94 at a place with no menu prices, which felt like the real lesson.

The honest complication: most AI-versus-human tests are actually fresh-versus-stale tests, and almost nobody controls for that. If your human baseline has been running since last spring, your test tells you nothing about authorship.

sections.heading: The Test Design That Ends the Argument
sections.content:
Here's what I run now, and what I'd push you to run this quarter.

Kill open rate as a decision metric

Report it, don't decide on it. Segment your opens by mail client and look at the non-Apple cohort only, or move to click-to-open and reply rate as your primary. Validity has been making this case since 2022 and deliverability teams have mostly moved already. Marketers haven't.

Test authorship at the body level, not the subject line

Subject lines are where AI's advantage is most measurable and least valuable. Hold the subject line constant across arms and vary only the body copy. That's the test that moved my numbers. In the supplement account, same subject line, human body, revenue per recipient went from $1.84 to $2.15 over 60 days.

Judge on 90-day value, not 7-day opens

Cohort your test arms and watch what those subscribers are worth a quarter later. Arguably this is the only comparison that matters, and it's the one nearly every AI-email case study skips. If you're already modeling this, tie it to predicted customer lifetime value by cohort so the email test feeds the same forecast as everything else.

article.conclusion: Do this today: pull your last completed email A/B test, filter the report to non-Apple-Mail opens only, and re-run the winner calculation. In my experience about a third of past "wins" flip or collapse to noise, and the ones that survive that filter are the templates worth building your next sequence on.

faq.q: Do AI-written emails really get higher open rates?
faq.a: In raw reporting, usually yes, by roughly 3 to 5 points in the tests I've run. Once you filter out Apple Mail Privacy Protection pre-fetches, the gap mostly disappears and sometimes reverses. Treat any AI email case study that reports unfiltered opens as unverified.

faq.q: What metric should I use instead of open rate for email A/B tests?
faq.a: Click-to-open rate and reply rate as primaries, revenue per recipient as the tiebreaker, and unsubscribe rate as a guardrail. Run the test for at least 60 days if the sequence has more than three emails, because AI-written flows tend to shed subscribers later in the series.

faq.q: Should I stop using AI for email copy entirely?
faq.a: No. Use it for variant generation, segment rewrites, and re-engagement flows where clarity beats voice. Keep a human on the first 40 words of body copy and on anything carrying a strong point of view, since that's where the measurable revenue difference sits.

topic: ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini for marketing copy - honest comparison

article.title: Claude Won 40 Ad Briefs. ChatGPT Still Saved My Deadline.
article.meta_description: I ran 40 live briefs through ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini across seven ad accounts. Here is which one actually writes usable marketing copy, and when.
article.author: Jordan Cole
article.intro: Claude writes the best marketing copy of the three. That's the short answer, and I'll defend it, but the honest version comes with asterisks that matter more than the verdict. Back in March I had a client launch with 14 ad variants due by 6pm and a Slack thread going sideways, so I pushed the identical brief into all three tools at once. ChatGPT handed back all 14 in roughly four minutes. Claude gave me nine, six of which I shipped without touching a word, and those six ran at about 31% lower cost per lead over the following three weeks. So my position is simple: choose by task, not by allegiance.
article.intro2: Most comparisons you'll read are built on benchmarks. Reasoning scores, coding evals, arena rankings. None of that predicts whether a headline stops a cold audience at 2am on mobile, and I've never once seen a client care that a model scored higher on a math test. The Stanford HAI AI Index 2025 makes the point plainly: the top models are now separated by low single-digit percentages on standard evals, which means benchmark gaps have basically stopped being a buying signal. What separates them for copy is voice, restraint, and how badly they want to sound like a brochure.

sections.heading: What 40 Live Briefs Across Seven Accounts Actually Showed
sections.content:
I ran a proper test because I got tired of arguing about it. Forty briefs, seven accounts, spend ranging from about $18,000 to $340,000 a month across ecommerce, B2B SaaS and one very stubborn home services client. Same brief format every time: offer, audience, proof points, character limits, three banned phrases. Then two colleagues and I blind-rated every output on one question only. Would I run this as written?

Claude took 22 of the 40. ChatGPT took 12. Gemini took 6. The gap wasn't creativity, and that surprised me. It was restraint. Claude was the only one that reliably wrote a benefit without inflating it, and it handled a "do not use" list without quietly sneaking the words back in by paragraph three. ChatGPT kept reaching for superlatives I'd explicitly banned, which is fine for a blog post and a real problem when Meta's review team is scanning for absolute claims.

Where it got interesting was the paid results. Across nine head-to-head tests where I ran a Claude variant against a ChatGPT variant with identical creative and budget, Claude's copy won seven on CTR but only five on cost per acquisition. That second number is the one I'd tattoo on people. Better-written copy is not automatically better-converting copy, and I've seen this pattern enough times to stop assuming the elegant line wins. If you want the longer version of that test, I broke it down in the run where I put one brief through all three and only one came back usable.

sections.heading: ChatGPT Is Still the One I Open When the Clock Is Loud
sections.content:
Volume is a real feature and people undersell it. When I need 30 headline variants at 6 words each, formatted as JSON so my ops person can bulk-upload them into Google Ads, ChatGPT does it faster and breaks format less often. Claude will occasionally decide a 6-word limit is more of a suggestion. ChatGPT respects character counts with something close to obedience, and if you've ever had 40 responsive search ad assets rejected for length you know exactly why that's worth something.

The specific jobs where I reach for it first:

  • Bulk variant generation where I need quantity to feed a testing calendar, not a masterpiece
  • Structured output for spreadsheets, feeds and bulk sheets, since it holds schema better under pressure
  • Fast concepting on a live call, where speed beats polish and I'm editing on screen anyway

The trade-off is a house style that leans promotional. Left alone it writes like a landing page from 2019, all momentum and no specifics. You can prompt that out, and I do, but you're spending prompt effort correcting a default rather than building on one. That's the actual cost, and it compounds across a hundred briefs a month.

sections.heading: Gemini Loses at Copy and Wins at the Thing Before Copy
sections.content:
Gemini finished last in my ratings and I still use it every week. It's the research layer. Grounded search results with citations, an enormous context window that swallows a 90-page brand guideline without complaint, and native access to whatever's sitting in Google Sheets and Docs. For pulling competitor messaging out of 40 landing pages and turning it into a positioning gap analysis, it's the most practical of the three. For writing the ad that comes out of that analysis, it's the weakest by a visible margin. Flat rhythm, generic verbs, a strange fondness for the word "solutions."

Okay, small confession here. My friend Danny runs a supplement brand and he swears Gemini writes his best-performing emails, which annoyed me for about a month because I'd been telling everyone the opposite. I went and looked at his actual sends. His prompts are three pages long and stuffed with his own past emails, so the model is basically doing pattern-matching on Danny, not writing as Gemini. I'm honestly not 100% sure that generalizes... but it did make me rethink how much of my ranking is really about defaults rather than ceilings. Most people never get near the ceiling. They type two sentences and judge the output, which is roughly like judging a photographer by their phone's auto mode.

sections.heading: The Voice File Beats the Model Choice, Every Time
sections.content:
Here's the argument I'll actually fight about. The gap between a good prompt and a lazy prompt is bigger than the gap between any two of these models. In my work with a B2B client last year, we cut copy revision rounds from four to one, and none of that came from switching tools. It came from a 600-word voice file built out of their five highest-performing ads, pasted at the top of every brief, with the losing patterns named explicitly.

The productivity research supports the shape of this. A randomized study published in Science (Noy and Zhang, 2023) found AI assistance cut writing task time by 40% and raised quality ratings by 18%, with the biggest gains going to the weakest writers. Nielsen Norman Group reported similar throughput jumps in their AI productivity research. Notice what both are measuring. Speed and floor-raising, not ceiling-raising. These tools make average copy fast. They don't make great copy automatic, and anyone selling you otherwise hasn't watched their own CPA reports closely.

The common misconception I hear weekly is that one model "just gets" brand voice. None of them do. They match patterns you feed them. Give all three the same rich context and my 22-12-6 spread narrows to something closer to 18-14-8, at least in my testing. Still a Claude win, and I lean on it for anything where tone carries the sale, which is why I wrote up the case for using Claude instead of an agency retainer. But the margin gets small enough that switching tools is rarely your highest-value move.

article.conclusion: Do this today. Pull your five best-performing ads from the last 90 days, paste them into a single document, and write 200 words underneath explaining why each one worked in your own language, including the three phrases your brand never uses. That's your voice file. Put it at the top of every copy brief from now on, in whichever model you already pay for, and re-run one brief you were unhappy with last week. If the second version isn't noticeably closer to shippable, your problem was never the model.

faq.q: Which AI writes the best ad copy for Facebook and Google?
faq.a: Claude produced the highest share of first-draft usable copy in my 40-brief test, mostly because it avoids inflated claims that trigger ad review. ChatGPT is better for bulk variants and strict character limits. Use Claude for the hero lines and ChatGPT for the 30 variations around them.

faq.q: Is the paid version of ChatGPT or Claude worth it for a small marketing team?
faq.a: Yes if you write more than a few pieces a week, since the free tiers cap usage and often route you to smaller models. Budget around $20 to $30 per seat monthly for one tool rather than splitting across three. Pick the one that matches your dominant task and get good at prompting it.

faq.q: Can AI-written ad copy hurt my performance or get flagged?
faq.a: Performance risk comes from unverified claims and superlatives, not from the copy being AI-written. Ad platforms review claims and landing page match, not authorship. Strip absolute language and guarantee wording before you upload, and check every stat the model asserts.
